questions.rationale: The opposite is wrong because the getter is specified to return '#' plus the fragment; only slice(1)/substring(1) removes it.

query.explanation: 'notexample.com'.endsWith('example.com') is true because the comparison ignores label boundaries. A domain allow-list must compare the full hostname, or require a dot prefix such as hostname === 'example.com' || hostname.endsWith('.example.com').
query.title: endsWith allows sibling domains

questions.rationale: It cannot be false: the final characters of notexample.com are exactly example.com, and endsWith does no DNS-label boundary check, so the attacker domain passes.

questions.prompt: Which check returns false for every entry in untrusted and true for allowed?

choices.rationale: //evil.example begins with a slash, so this check accepts the protocol-relative payload.
/\evil.example does not start with //, yet the parser normalizes the backslash and resolves it to evil.example.
Both https://app.example@evil.example and https://app.example.evil.com contain that substring while pointing elsewhere.

query.explanation: String-level checks miss at least one bypass: a leading // is still a slash, a backslash normalizes to a slash, userinfo smuggles a trusted-looking label, and a substring match hits lookalike domains. Resolving the target against the base and comparing the resulting origin handles all four while still allowing /dashboard.
query.title: resolve, then compare origins

questions.prompt: does the parsed target satisfy this http scheme allow list?
questions.code:
const u = new URL('javascript:alert(1)', 'https://app.example/');
console.log(u.protocol === 'https:' || u.protocol === 'http:');

query.explanation: javascript:alert(1) is an absolute URL, so the base is ignored and u.protocol is 'javascript:'. Neither branch of the allow-list matches, so the check prints false. This is why redirect code should test the parsed protocol rather than assume a relative string.
query.title: scheme allow-list on a parsed redirect target

questions.rationale: True would require the base scheme to win, but the target already has its own scheme, so protocol is 'javascript:' and both comparisons fail.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?

choices.rationale: The check runs on the percent-encoded text, which starts with '%', so the blocking branch is never taken.
The accepted branch calls decodeURIComponent, so the %2F sequences are turned back into slashes before printing.
Both %2F escapes decode, producing two slashes rather than one.

query.explanation: The guard inspects the still-encoded string, where %2F%2F does not look like //, so the target passes. decodeURIComponent then turns it back into //evil.example/x, the very protocol-relative value the check was meant to stop. Always decode (and resolve) first, then validate.
query.title: validating before decoding

questions.prompt: What does this code print?

choices.rationale: The fragment is exposed as u.hash and is never concatenated, so #x is dropped.
The relative target inherits the base origin, so the origin comparison matches and the fallback is not used.
Only pathname and search are returned, so no scheme or host appears in the result.

query.explanation: The target resolves to https://app.example/dash?a=1#x, whose origin matches the base, so the function returns only the pathname plus search. The fragment lives in u.hash and is therefore dropped, which is the point of rebuilding the value from parsed components instead of echoing user input.
query.title: rebuilding a same-origin redirect target

questions.prompt: Does this protocol-relative redirect target keep the user on the base URL's host?

query.explanation: A target beginning with `//` is a protocol-relative URL: resolution keeps the base scheme but replaces the authority, so `//evil.example/pwn` becomes `https://evil.example/pwn`. Validators that only reject strings starting with `http://` or `https://`, or that treat any leading `/` as "local", are bypassed by this form. Compare the resolved `origin` against an allow-list instead of inspecting the raw string.
query.title: Protocol-relative redirect targets

questions.rationale: Answering True is wrong because `//` starts a new authority: the resolved host is evil.example, not redirect.example, even though only the scheme was inherited.

questions.prompt: What does this code print?

choices.rationale: `trusted.example` sits before the `@`, so it is parsed as the userinfo (username), and is available via `u.username`, not `u.hostname`.
`hostname` never includes userinfo; the `@` and everything before it are stripped out of the host component during parsing.
The URL is valid and has a real authority, so parsing succeeds and `hostname` is populated rather than empty.

query.explanation: Everything between `//` and the first `@` is the userinfo component, not the host. So in `https://trusted.example@evil.example/login` the browser connects to evil.example and exposes `trusted.example` only as a username. Checks like `target.includes("trusted.example")` or `startsWith("https://trusted.example")` pass while the user lands on the attacker's site. Always read `hostname`/`origin` from a parsed URL.
query.title: Userinfo in redirect targets

questions.prompt: Which target value makes safe() return true?

choices.rationale: Its origin is `http://app.example`, which is a different string from the allow-listed `https://app.example`, and the protocol check also fails.
The protocol-relative form resolves to origin `https://app.example.evil.test`, an attacker host that is not in the allow-list.
`app.example` here is only a label prefix of a different registrable domain, so the origin `https://app.example.evil.test` is not allow-listed.

query.explanation: Resolving the target against the application base and comparing the full `origin` string is the robust pattern: the origin is scheme + host + port, so scheme downgrades, sibling domains and protocol-relative authorities all produce a value that is absent from the allow-list. A relative path such as `/dashboard?next=2` resolves to `https://app.example/dashboard?next=2`, whose origin matches, so it is the only accepted target here.
query.title: Origin allow-lists for redirects

questions.prompt: Which directive applies to script loading under this header?

choices.rationale: img-src only covers image loads; it is never consulted for script requests.
script-src-elem is not declared in this header, so it cannot supply a source list.

choices.text: no directive applies, so the script loads unrestricted
choices.rationale: A missing script-src falls back to default-src instead of leaving scripts unrestricted.

query.explanation: Fetch directives such as script-src, img-src and connect-src fall back to default-src when they are absent. Here no script-src (or script-src-elem) is declared, so script requests are checked against default-src's list ('self' https:). Only a few directives, like frame-ancestors and base-uri, have no default-src fallback.
query.title: Directive fallback to default-src

questions.prompt: Does a plain inline script with no nonce attribute run under this policy?

query.explanation: When a script-src list contains at least one nonce-source or hash-source, browsers ignore 'unsafe-inline' entirely. That makes the policy backward compatible with old browsers while modern ones require a matching nonce or hash, so a plain inline script with no nonce is blocked here.
query.title: Nonces override 'unsafe-inline'

questions.rationale: 'unsafe-inline' is discarded as soon as a nonce-source or hash-source appears, so the un-nonced inline script is blocked rather than allowed.

questions.prompt: Which image URL does this policy allow?

choices.rationale: The wildcard requires at least one subdomain label, so the bare host example.com is not matched.
The real host here is evil.net; matching compares host labels from the right, not substrings.
Only the host is matched against the source; the path is irrelevant to this source expression.

query.explanation: A wildcard host-source like *.example.com matches hosts that have at least one extra label in front of example.com, so cdn.example.com matches but the bare registrable domain example.com does not. The wildcard also never matches a host that merely contains the string, such as cdn.example.com.evil.net.
query.title: Wildcard host-source matching

questions.prompt: Which script-src source list does the browser enforce for this header?

choices.rationale: The later duplicate is dropped, not preferred; the first script-src wins.
Duplicate directives in one policy are not merged into a union of sources.

choices.text: none, because duplicates invalidate the whole policy
choices.rationale: A duplicate directive is ignored with a warning; the rest of the policy stays in force.

query.explanation: Within a single policy, a directive name may appear only once. Browsers keep the first occurrence, ignore every later duplicate, and usually log a console warning. So script-src here is just 'self' and the cdn origin is never allowed.
query.title: Duplicate directives inside one policy

questions.prompt: Does this img-src scheme source allow the http image URL below?

query.explanation: The scheme-source https: allows any host but only over the https scheme. An http:// URL does not match, so the image is blocked. Note the reverse is asymmetric: a source of http: would also permit https URLs, because CSP treats https as a secure upgrade of http.
query.title: Scheme-source matching

questions.rationale: https: restricts loads to the https scheme, so the plain http image URL fails the check and is blocked.

questions.prompt: Which script origins can load when both headers are sent?

choices.rationale: Separate policies are not unioned; a load must pass every policy that is enforced.
These origins are each missing from one of the two policies, so each is blocked by that policy.

choices.text: no origin, because the two headers conflict
choices.rationale: Two headers never cancel out; they are both applied and the effective set is their intersection.

questions.code:
Content-Security-Policy: script-src https://a.example https://b.example
Content-Security-Policy: script-src https://b.example https://c.example

query.explanation: Each Content-Security-Policy header creates a separate policy, and a resource must satisfy every one of them. The practical result is the intersection of the source lists, so only https://b.example can load scripts here. Adding a header can only tighten, never loosen, an existing policy.
query.title: Multiple CSP headers are enforced independently

questions.prompt: How many directives does this meta policy declare?

choices.rationale: The semicolons separate three independent directives, not one long source list.
connect-src is a third directive alongside default-src and script-src.
There are only three semicolon-separated segments; https://api.example.com is a source, not a directive.

query.explanation: A policy delivered in a meta element lives in the content attribute as semicolon-separated directives, each starting with a directive name followed by its source list. Splitting on ';' and dropping empty segments counts three directives here: default-src, script-src and connect-src.
query.title: Reading a policy from a meta element

questions.prompt: Which directive in this meta policy does the browser ignore?

choices.rationale: script-src is fully supported in a meta-delivered policy and is enforced here.
img-src works the same in meta as in a header, so the https: restriction applies.

choices.text: none of them, meta and header policies behave identically
choices.rationale: frame-ancestors, report-uri/report-to and sandbox are all ignored in meta-delivered policies.

query.explanation: frame-ancestors, report-uri/report-to and sandbox are ignored when the policy is delivered in a meta element, because the document has already begun loading and framing decisions are made by the response headers. To stop framing you must send frame-ancestors in the Content-Security-Policy HTTP header.
query.title: Directives that only work in a header

questions.prompt: Does 'self' allow this script URL for a page served from https://app.example.com?

query.explanation: 'self' matches only the document's own origin: the same scheme, host and port. A sibling subdomain like cdn.example.com is a different origin, so the script is blocked. Allowing it requires listing https://cdn.example.com (or a wildcard such as *.example.com) explicitly.
query.title: What 'self' actually matches

questions.rationale: 'self' is an exact origin match, not a domain-suffix match, so cdn.example.com is a different origin and the load is blocked.

questions.prompt: Which source in this script-src list takes effect?

choices.rationale: 'strict-dynamic' makes browsers ignore host-source and scheme-source entries like this one.
'unsafe-inline' is dropped both by the presence of a nonce and by 'strict-dynamic'.
'strict-dynamic' deliberately neutralises the allowlist and 'unsafe-inline', leaving only nonce/hash sources.

query.explanation: When 'strict-dynamic' is present, browsers ignore every host-source and scheme-source plus 'unsafe-inline', leaving only nonce and hash sources. Scripts that pass the nonce check may then create further scripts programmatically, which is what makes the policy workable without an allowlist.
query.title: 'strict-dynamic' discards host and scheme sources

questions.prompt: What value does the browser store for the cookie named pref?

choices.rationale: Only the first segment of the value; the value is not split again at later '=' characters.
This drops the leading 'a=' by splitting at the wrong '='; the split happens at the first '=' in the whole pair.
That is the full name/value pair; the stored value excludes the cookie name and the first '='.

query.explanation: A Set-Cookie header is split at the first semicolon to get the name/value pair, and that pair is split at the FIRST '=' only. Everything after that first '=' up to the semicolon is the value, so extra '=' characters stay in the value verbatim.
query.title: Set-Cookie name/value split

questions.prompt: Is a cookie set with Path=/app sent on a request to /application/data?

query.explanation: Path matching is not plain string prefixing: the request path must equal the cookie path, or the character right after the cookie path in the request path must be '/'. '/application/data' continues with 'l', so /app does not match.
query.title: Cookie path matching

questions.rationale: A 'true' answer assumes raw prefix matching, but the path-match algorithm requires a '/' boundary after the cookie path, and '/application/data' has 'l' there.

questions.prompt: Which Set-Cookie header satisfies the __Host- prefix rules?

choices.rationale: A Domain attribute is forbidden for __Host- cookies, so the browser rejects this header.
The Secure attribute is missing, which __Host- cookies require.
__Host- cookies must use Path=/ exactly; any narrower path is rejected.

query.explanation: A cookie whose name starts with __Host- is only accepted if it is marked Secure, has Path=/ exactly, and carries no Domain attribute. That pins the cookie to the single host that set it and blocks subdomain injection.
query.title: __Host- cookie prefix

questions.prompt: Is a SameSite=Lax cookie sent on a cross-site top-level GET navigation?

query.explanation: Lax withholds the cookie from cross-site subresource requests and unsafe methods, but allows it on top-level navigations made with a safe method such as GET. Only SameSite=Strict blocks that case too.
query.title: SameSite=Lax on navigations

questions.rationale: Answering false describes SameSite=Strict; Lax deliberately keeps cookies on cross-site top-level GET navigations so that following a link keeps the user logged in.

questions.prompt: Which host does a cookie with Domain=example.com NOT get sent to?

choices.rationale: A direct subdomain matches Domain=example.com, so it does receive the cookie.
The domain itself always matches its own Domain attribute.
Domain matching covers subdomains at any depth, so this host receives the cookie.

query.explanation: Domain matching accepts the domain itself and any host that ends with '.' plus that domain. A host that merely contains the string, like example.com.evil.net, is a different registrable domain and never receives the cookie.
query.title: Cookie domain matching

questions.prompt: Does document.cookie expose the Path and SameSite attributes of a stored cookie?

query.explanation: Attributes are only meaningful when writing. Reading document.cookie returns just a list of 'name=value' pairs separated by '; ', with no Path, Domain, Secure, Expires or SameSite information.
query.title: document.cookie is write-only for attributes

questions.rationale: Answering true confuses the setter with the getter: attributes are parsed when assigning, but the getter only returns name=value pairs.

questions.prompt: Which attribute determines this cookie's lifetime?

choices.rationale: Expires is ignored whenever a valid Max-Age is also present.

choices.text: Whichever appears last in the header
choices.rationale: Precedence is fixed by the attribute name, not by position in the header.
Session lifetime applies only when neither Max-Age nor Expires is given.

questions.code: Set-Cookie: sid=9; Expires=Fri, 01 Jan 2027 00:00:00 GMT; Max-Age=600

query.explanation: When both are present, Max-Age takes precedence over Expires regardless of the order they appear in, so the cookie lives 600 seconds rather than until 2027.
query.title: Max-Age beats Expires

questions.prompt: What does get('session') return?

choices.rationale: That is the real session cookie, but the substring search matches the earlier 'x_session=' first and never reaches it.
The slice starts after the matched 'session=' text, so the name prefix is not included.
A match is found (inside x_session), so the function returns a string rather than undefined.

query.explanation: indexOf('session=') first matches inside 'x_session=', so the helper reads an attacker-controlled decoy cookie. Safe lookups split the jar on '; ' and compare whole names, or use a regex with a boundary.
query.title: Substring cookie lookup is unsafe

questions.prompt: Can a page served over http successfully set a cookie that carries the Secure attribute?

query.explanation: Under the strict secure cookie rules, a non-secure origin may not create or update a cookie with the Secure attribute; the write is rejected. Secure cookies can only be written from an https page.
query.title: Strict secure cookies

questions.rationale: Answering true reflects old behaviour; modern browsers reject Secure cookie writes from insecure origins so a plain http page cannot create one.

questions.prompt: Which of these Set-Cookie headers does the browser reject?

choices.rationale: SameSite=None is paired with Secure here, which is exactly what the rule demands.
Lax is a valid same-site restriction and never requires Secure to be accepted.
Strict cookies are accepted without Secure; only SameSite=None forces the Secure attribute.

query.explanation: Cross-site cookies must opt in with SameSite=None, and that value is only honoured together with Secure. A SameSite=None cookie without Secure is dropped entirely.
query.title: SameSite=None requires Secure

questions.prompt: Which of these cross-origin requests triggers a CORS preflight?

choices.text: GET with only an Accept header
choices.rationale: GET is a safelisted method and Accept is a safelisted request header, so this is a simple request.
That media type is one of the three safelisted Content-Type values, so no preflight is needed.
HEAD is safelisted and there are no non-safelisted headers, so the request goes out directly.

query.explanation: A request skips the preflight only if the method is GET, HEAD or POST, every header is CORS-safelisted, and any Content-Type is application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data or text/plain. application/json falls outside that list, so the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight carrying Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers.
query.title: Simple requests vs preflighted requests

questions.prompt: What Origin header value does a request from this page URL carry?

choices.rationale: 443 is the default port for https, so origin serialization omits it.
An origin is only scheme, host and port; the path is never part of it.
The scheme is part of the origin, so the bare host is not a valid serialization.

query.explanation: The Origin header holds the serialized origin of the requesting document: scheme, host and, only when non-default, the port. Path, query and fragment are stripped, and a default port such as 443 for https or 80 for http is omitted. new URL(href).origin performs exactly this serialization.
query.title: Serializing an origin for the Origin header

questions.prompt: Which response header is readable by script without Access-Control-Expose-Headers?

choices.rationale: Custom headers are hidden on CORS responses until the server lists them in Access-Control-Expose-Headers.
Set-Cookie is a forbidden response header name that script can never read, even same-origin.
Authorization is not a CORS-safelisted response header, so it is not exposed by default.

query.explanation: The default readable set on a CORS response is Cache-Control, Content-Language, Content-Length, Content-Type, Expires, Last-Modified and Pragma. Content-Language belongs to that list, so headers.get('Content-Language') works with no extra server configuration, while anything else needs Access-Control-Expose-Headers.
query.title: CORS-safelisted response headers

questions.prompt: Which of these headers sets the preflight cache lifetime?

choices.rationale: Cache-Control governs the HTTP cache for normal responses, not the separate CORS preflight cache.
No such header exists in the CORS specification.
Expires is an HTTP caching header and is ignored when the browser stores a preflight result.

questions.code:
// OPTIONS response headers
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: PUT
Access-Control-Max-Age: 600
Cache-Control: no-store
Expires: 0

query.explanation: Access-Control-Max-Age gives the seconds a browser may reuse an OPTIONS result for the same origin, URL, method and header set, skipping further preflights. Only that header feeds the preflight cache; browsers also clamp the value to their own maximum, so a huge number does not guarantee a long-lived entry.
query.title: Caching a preflight result

questions.prompt: Which header combination lets script read this credentialed cross-origin response?

choices.rationale: The wildcard origin is rejected outright for credentialed requests, whatever Allow-Credentials says.
Without Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true the browser discards a credentialed response.
This fails twice over: wildcard origin and missing Allow-Credentials.

query.explanation: For credentials: 'include' the server must echo the exact request origin in Access-Control-Allow-Origin and send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Both conditions are necessary; failing either makes the browser block the response even though the server already processed the request. Add Vary: Origin when echoing the origin so caches do not mix responses.
query.title: Credentialed CORS requires an exact origin

questions.prompt: Which Access-Control-Allow-Methods value permits a non-credentialed PATCH request?

choices.rationale: PATCH is absent from the list, so the preflight fails.
Method matching is byte-case-sensitive, so lowercase patch does not match the PATCH request method.
ANY is not a method name and has no special meaning; only the literal * acts as a wildcard.

query.explanation: On a non-credentialed preflight the literal * in Access-Control-Allow-Methods matches any method, so PATCH is approved. Explicit lists must spell the method exactly, uppercase included, since matching is case-sensitive. For credentialed requests the wildcard loses its special meaning and PATCH must be listed by name.
query.title: Wildcards in Access-Control-Allow-Methods

questions.prompt: Which request header does the preflight for this fetch include?

choices.rationale: That is the response header the server uses to approve headers; the browser never sends it.
It is sent on the preflight, but it carries the method (PUT), not the header names.
Origin carries the requesting page's scheme/host/port, not the list of request headers.

query.explanation: A non-simple request triggers an OPTIONS preflight. The browser announces the intended method in Access-Control-Request-Method and the comma-separated, lowercased list of non-safelisted request headers (here content-type with a JSON value plus x-token) in Access-Control-Request-Headers. Access-Control-Allow-* names are response headers the server sends back, not request headers.
query.title: Preflight request headers

questions.prompt: Which Access-Control-Allow-Credentials value lets script read a credentialed response?

choices.rationale: The comparison is case-sensitive, so a capitalised value does not match and the response stays blocked.
The header is not boolean-ish; only the literal string true is accepted.
Not a recognised value; the check fails and credentials are not exposed.

query.explanation: Access-Control-Allow-Credentials is compared byte-for-byte against the lowercase string "true". Any other value, including "True", "1", or "yes", is treated as a failure and the browser blocks the credentialed response.
query.title: Access-Control-Allow-Credentials value

questions.prompt: Which X-Frame-Options value blocks framing by all sites, including the page's own origin?

choices.rationale: SAMEORIGIN still permits a page on the identical origin to frame the document.
Modern browsers ignore ALLOW-FROM, so the response ends up with no framing restriction at all.
ALLOWALL is not a defined token; browsers treat the invalid header as absent and allow framing.

query.explanation: DENY refuses framing from any ancestor, even a same-origin one. SAMEORIGIN only refuses cross-origin ancestors. ALLOW-FROM was dropped by modern browsers and unknown tokens like ALLOWALL are invalid, so both leave the page framable.
query.title: X-Frame-Options values

questions.prompt: Does the sandbox attribute below let the framed document run scripts?

query.explanation: A sandbox attribute turns every restriction on, then each listed token lifts one restriction. Without allow-scripts the framed document cannot execute script, no matter which other tokens are present.
query.title: iframe sandbox tokens

questions.rationale: Scripting stays disabled because the token list has no allow-scripts entry; allow-same-origin only restores the document's real origin.

questions.prompt: Is the framed window's top property the same object as the embedding window here?

query.explanation: top always references the outermost browsing context of the chain. For a one-level-deep frame inside a top-level page, the child's top is the embedding window, which is why top !== self is the classic in-a-frame test.
query.title: window.top in a frame

questions.rationale: The embedding document is itself the top-level browsing context, so the child's top points straight back at it rather than at the child.

questions.prompt: Which embedding origin does this frame-ancestors list allow?

choices.rationale: https://*.partner.example covers subdomains only; the bare registrable host does not match the wildcard.
'self' includes the scheme, so the http version of the same host is a different origin and is rejected.
The host ends in evil.com, so it is not a subdomain of partner.example despite the shared label.

questions.code:
// page served from https://app.example.com
// Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' https://*.partner.example

query.explanation: 'self' matches only the page's own scheme, host and port. A wildcard host pattern matches subdomains of the suffix but not the bare suffix itself, and never a domain that merely contains the suffix as a label prefix.
query.title: CSP frame-ancestors matching

questions.prompt: Which framing policy does a modern browser enforce when both headers are sent?

choices.rationale: The legacy header is ignored once frame-ancestors is present in the policy.

choices.text: both, with DENY winning as the stricter rule
choices.rationale: Browsers do not intersect the two mechanisms; frame-ancestors simply replaces X-Frame-Options.

choices.text: neither; the conflicting headers disable framing checks
choices.rationale: A conflict never disables protection; the CSP directive is still applied normally.

query.explanation: When a CSP contains frame-ancestors, browsers enforce it and ignore X-Frame-Options entirely. The two are not combined, so a loose frame-ancestors value can effectively override a strict legacy header.
query.title: frame-ancestors versus X-Frame-Options

questions.prompt: Which sandbox value lets a frame run scripts while keeping it in an opaque origin?

choices.rationale: allow-same-origin restores the real origin, so the frame is no longer isolated and can script its way out of the sandbox.
Without allow-scripts the frame cannot run any script, and it also keeps its real origin.
An empty sandbox applies every restriction, so scripting stays blocked.

query.explanation: allow-scripts re-enables scripting, while omitting allow-same-origin keeps the framed document in an opaque origin so it cannot reach the embedder's storage or DOM. Granting both tokens together lets sandboxed content remove its own sandbox.
query.title: allow-scripts without allow-same-origin

questions.prompt: Does the frame below block form submission from the embedded document?

query.explanation: sandbox with no value is the most restrictive setting: scripts, forms, popups, plugins and same-origin access are all disabled until specific tokens are added.
query.title: empty sandbox attribute

questions.rationale: A valueless sandbox attribute parses to an empty token list, so no restriction is lifted and allow-forms is absent, which keeps form submission blocked.

questions.prompt: How many sandbox tokens apply to this frame?

choices.rationale: Two distinct tokens are present, allow-scripts and allow-forms.
Ordered-set parsing removes the duplicate allow-scripts instead of counting it twice.
Only three whitespace-separated words appear, and one of them repeats.

query.explanation: The sandbox attribute is parsed as an ordered set of space-separated tokens, which drops duplicates. Repeating allow-scripts therefore adds nothing and the list holds two tokens.
query.title: sandbox token list parsing

questions.prompt: Does this SAMEORIGIN policy allow the listed embedding page to frame the document?

query.explanation: SAMEORIGIN requires the ancestor's origin to match the framed document's origin on scheme, host and port. Sharing only the host is not enough.
query.title: SAMEORIGIN compares full origins

questions.rationale: An origin comparison includes the scheme, so the http embedder is cross-origin to the https document and SAMEORIGIN rejects it.

questions.prompt: Which check tells a document that it is running inside a frame?

choices.rationale: That is true in a top-level page and false inside a frame, so it is the inverted test.
length counts child frames, so a top-level page that embeds a frame also passes this check.
referrer reflects navigation history, not nesting; a framed document can have an empty referrer.

query.explanation: Comparing top with self is the reliable test: in a framed document top is an ancestor window, while in a top-level page top and self are the same object. The other expressions are either true in the top-level page too or unrelated to nesting.
query.title: detecting a framed document

choices.rationale: JSON is not on the CORS safelist, so it turns the request into a preflighted one.
Only form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data, and text/plain are safelisted; XML is not.
text/html is not safelisted even though it is a text type, so a preflight is still sent.

questions.prompt: Which Content-Type on this cross-origin POST avoids a CORS preflight?

query.explanation: A cross-origin POST stays a simple request only when Content-Type is one of the three safelisted values: application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data, or text/plain. Any other media type makes Content-Type a non-safelisted request header, so the browser sends an OPTIONS preflight first and waits for Access-Control-Allow-Headers to permit it.
query.title: Safelisted Content-Type values

questions.prompt: Can script read a credentialed CORS response whose allow-origin header is a wildcard?

query.explanation: When a request carries credentials, the wildcard is not allowed: the server must echo the exact requesting origin in Access-Control-Allow-Origin (plus send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true). With `*`, the browser fails the CORS check and the fetch promise rejects, so script reads nothing.
query.title: Wildcard origin with credentials

questions.rationale: A credentialed request requires the exact origin to be echoed back; `*` fails the check even when Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true is present, so the response stays unreadable.
